questions.q: Why is hardcoding a specific record Id (e.g. '001xx000003DGb2AAG') inside a test method considered a serious mistake?
options: Apex does not allow string literals that look like Ids
Salesforce Ids are not portable across orgs, so the test fails in any org where that exact record doesn't exist
It always triggers a governor limit violation
It automatically disables code coverage for that class
questions.explain: A hardcoded Id depends on one specific org's exact data existing at one specific moment — it fails the instant the test runs in a different org or the record is deleted.

questions.q: What is the correct way for a test to obtain the Id of a record it needs, instead of hardcoding one?
options: Query for any record of that type and hope one exists
Ask the admin to provide a fixed Id for every sandbox
Use Test.isRunningTest() to generate a fake Id
Create the record inside the test itself (directly, via @TestSetup, or via a factory) and use the Id from that insert
questions.explain: The reliable fix is to create the needed record inside the test (or its setup) and capture the Id from that insert, so the test never depends on data that may or may not already exist.

questions.q: What makes 'System.assert(true);' as the only check in a test method dangerous?
options: It will cause a compile error
It automatically fails code coverage requirements
It is structurally guaranteed to pass no matter what the code under test actually does, so it proves nothing while still showing a green result
It is not valid Apex syntax
questions.explain: Since the condition is hardcoded true, this assertion can never fail regardless of the code's actual behavior — the test appears to 'pass' while verifying nothing, and this is easy to overlook in a quick code review.

questions.q: A test assumes an Opportunity's StageName picklist includes a value called 'Qualification' without creating or checking for it. What's the risk?
options: In an org whose sales process doesn't include that exact stage value, the test fails for a reason unrelated to whether the code under test is correct
None — all Salesforce orgs share identical picklist values by law
Picklist fields cannot be set from Apex, so this code won't compile
This only matters for currency fields, not picklists
questions.explain: Picklist values are customizable per org; assuming a specific value exists without verifying it is an org-specific assumption that can make a test fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the actual code under test.

questions.q: What is the main risk of relying heavily on @isTest(SeeAllData=true) across a test suite, beyond its incompatibility with @TestSetup?
options: It makes test execution instantaneous with zero governor limits
It automatically increases the required coverage percentage to 100%
It tends to bake in assumptions about data that already exists in whichever org the tests happen to run against, which can quietly break as that data changes
It disables all assertion methods
questions.explain: Broad reliance on SeeAllData=true reintroduces a version of the hardcoded-data problem — tests end up depending on org data that can change or not exist elsewhere, undermining the portability that default test data isolation provides.
